Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

propose verb

ask someone to marry

also marriage proposal, proposal of marriage, propose to someone, ask for someone’s hand

classical

Plaut. Aul. 219: fīliam tuam mī uxōrem poscō
Plaut. Trin. 499: sine dōte poscō tuam sorōrem fīliō

uxōrem poscere

uxor, uxōris f., with poscō, poscere, poposcī; the woman in the accusative, the man in the dative

ask for (a woman’s) hand

Lewis & Short, s.v. poscō: “to demand one’s hand, ask in marriage”. The request went to the woman’s father, who promised her (dēspondēre).

Examples

  • quae rēs rēctē vortat mihique tibique tuaeque fīliae, fīliam tuam mī uxōrem poscō. prōmitte hoc fore.

    And may it turn out well for me and for you and for your daughter: I am asking for your daughter’s hand. Promise me it will be so.Plaut. Aul. 218–219

  • tū condiciōnem hanc accipe, auscultā mihi, atque eam dēspondē mī.

    Accept this proposal, listen to me, and promise her to me.Plaut. Aul. 237–238

Other words

  • condiciō, condiciōnis f. — a marriage proposal, a match

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Plaut. Aul. 237: tū condiciōnem hanc accipe; Plaut. Trin. 501: condiciōnem quojus modī

    Lewis & Short: “a marriage, match … (freq. and class.)”; in full, condiciō uxōria (Cic. Lael. 34).

  • dēspondeō, dēspondēre, dēspondī, dēspōnsum — promise in marriage (of the father); accept a proposal

    verb, second conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Aul. 238: atque eam dēspondē mī

See also marry, promise, propose.

SourcesLewis & Short: posco · Lewis & Short: condicio · Lewis & Short: despondeo
